title: How Should Distributors Choose a Government Sales Platform?
summary: What public sector distributors should test before picking a platform to find and share RFx.
body_markdown:
**Quick answer:** A public sector technology distributor should choose a government sales platform on three things: whether it can find demand for the manufacturers on your line card across federal, contract vehicle and state and local sources; whether it lets you share each request for quote, proposal or information (RFx) with the right reseller partner without buying that partner a seat; and whether it speeds up the quote requests partners send back to you. A platform built only to help one company bid will miss most of that work.


‍


## What does a distributor need that a reseller doesn't?


A reseller, or value-added reseller (VAR), wins orders and holds contract vehicles. A distributor usually sits one step back. It carries products from many original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), supplies them to dozens or hundreds of resellers, and grows when those partners win. That changes what "finding opportunities" means.


- **You sell through other companies' vehicles.** On GSA eBuy, for example, the[contractor job aid](https://ebuy.gsa.gov/ebuy/assets/content/eBuy-Contractor_jobaid.pdf) says holders "will not be able to view RFQs posted under SINs that are not in your contract." Demand on a vehicle is visible to its holders first, and a distributor sees it only when partners pass it along. We explain the wider pattern in[why contract vehicle RFQs don't appear on SAM.gov](https://www.govly.com/blog/contract-vehicle-rfqs-not-on-sam-gov) .
- **Your search starts with a line card, not a NAICS code.** You care about every solicitation that names a manufacturer or part you carry, whoever ends up bidding.
- **Your output is a handoff.** The goal is to put the right opportunity in front of the right partner, then turn their quote request around quickly.


Reseller criteria still matter, and we cover them in[how federal IT resellers should choose an RFQ platform](https://www.govly.com/blog/how-resellers-choose-rfq-platform) . For the broader market, see our[buyer's guide to government contracting software](https://www.govly.com/blog/best-government-contracting-software) . This guide covers what changes when you are the distributor.


‍


## What should a distributor look for in a government sales platform?


Use these six criteria. The first three decide whether a tool can do a distributor's job at all.


Criterion What to ask Why it matters for distributors


Line-card search Can I search by manufacturer, part number and product terms, including inside attachments? Part numbers often appear only in a bill of materials or spec sheet, not the notice title.


Source coverage Does one feed cover SAM.gov, contract vehicle RFQs and state and local sources? Your manufacturers' demand is split across all three.


Partner sharing Can I share an RFx with a reseller, and what does that partner need to view it? If every partner needs a paid seat, sharing stops at your biggest accounts.


Partner visibility Can partners share vehicle RFQs back with me, with their permission? That is how a distributor sees demand on vehicles it doesn't hold.


Quote intake How do reseller quote requests reach the right product manager or manufacturer team? Short RFQ windows leave little time for a request to sit in a shared inbox.


Security What has the vendor's environment been assessed against? Defense-focused partners may ask how shared files are protected.


### Why does line-card search come first?


A distributor carrying many manufacturers can't build one saved search per opportunity type. It needs searches that start from what it sells. Test this with real data: pick three manufacturers and ten part numbers from your line card, and ask the vendor to show matching solicitations from the last month, including ones where the part appears only in an attachment. If the tool searches titles and descriptions only, you will miss many product-specific requests.


### How should RFx sharing work?


Sharing should be quick for you and easy for the partner. Ask the vendor to share one live opportunity with a reseller contact during the demo. Check what that contact sees, whether they can add teammates, and whether they can comment or attach a quote without a new contract. Then ask the reverse: when a reseller holds a vehicle you don't, can they share its RFQs with you in a controlled way?


‍


## How does state and local work change the evaluation?


For many distributors, state, local and education (SLED) buying runs through cooperative contracts as much as open bids. NASPO ValuePoint is a common example. Its[buyer FAQ](https://www.naspovaluepoint.org/faqs-for-buyers/) says a lead state runs each solicitation, and that once awarded, master agreements "are available to all states, their political subdivisions, and other eligible entities." Each state then signs a participating addendum before its agencies buy.


That means a distributor needs two views. The first is open SLED solicitations from thousands of agency sites (see[what SLED means](https://www.govly.com/blog/what-does-sled-mean) ). The second is the cooperative contracts your resellers hold, and which states they can sell into. Ask each vendor whether cooperative contract solicitations appear in the same feed as federal work, or in a separate product.


‍


## Distributor evaluation checklist


- Bring three manufacturers and ten part numbers, and check matches inside attachments.
- Confirm federal, contract vehicle and SLED results appear in one feed.
- Share one live opportunity with a reseller and note what they need to open it.
- Ask how a reseller can share vehicle RFQs back with you.
- Trace one reseller quote request from arrival to the right person on your team.
- Ask which users need paid seats and which partners can view without one.
- Ask for the vendor's security assessment documentation.


‍

## FAQ


**Does a distributor need to hold its own contract vehicles?**
No. Many distributors reach government buyers mainly through resellers' vehicles, though some also hold schedules or cooperative contracts directly.


**Who at a distributor should own the platform?**
Usually the public sector or partner program team, with product or manufacturer managers owning the saved searches for their lines.


**Can OEMs and distributors use the same platform?**
Yes, and it helps when they do, because an opportunity can move from manufacturer to distributor to reseller without being re-entered at each step.


**How long should a distributor trial a platform?**
Long enough to see live requests across your top manufacturers and at least one busy vehicle, which for most teams means a few weeks rather than a single demo.
